title: An ordinary day
goal: Describe your daily routine from getting up to going to bed, use separable verbs, and recognize reflexive verbs.
bekal: tell the order of your day with *eerst*, *daarna*, *dan*
wave: Review **Unit 7**: order your breakfast, lunch and evening drink in Dutch, three times, at three different levels of politeness.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Hoe ziet jouw dag eruit?
dialogs.intro: In the university cafeteria. Sanne wonders why Budi always looks sleepy.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.id: What does your day look like?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ik sta om zes uur op. Veel te vroeg.
lines.id: I get up at six. Way too early.
lines.literal: I stand at six hour up. much too early.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ik douche, ik kleed me aan en ik ontbijt rustig.
lines.id: I shower, get dressed and have a relaxed breakfast.
lines.literal: I shower, I dress me on and I breakfast calmly.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Daarna pak ik de trein. Ik kom om half negen aan.
lines.id: After that I take the train. I get in at half past eight.
lines.literal: after-that take I the train. I come at half nine in.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Ik sta pas om acht uur op. De universiteit is om de hoek.
lines.id: I don't get up until eight. The university is just around the corner.
lines.literal: I stand only at eight hour up. the university is round the corner.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: En 's avonds? Wat doe je dan?
lines.id: And in the evening? What do you do then?
lines.literal: and of-the evening? what do you then?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ik kook, ik bel mijn ouders, en ik studeer nog wat.
lines.id: I cook, I call my parents, and I study a bit more.
lines.literal: I cook, I call my parents, and I study still some.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Hoe laat ga je naar bed?
lines.id: What time do you go to bed?
lines.literal: how late go you to bed?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Meestal rond middernacht. Daarom ben ik altijd moe.
lines.id: Usually around midnight. That's why I'm always tired.
lines.literal: mostly around midnight. therefore am I always tired.

notes: **Hoe ziet jouw dag eruit?** — from *eruitzien* (to look like), a separable verb that even has two parts. Learn the question as a whole; it's used all the time.

**Ik sta om zes uur op** — this is the typically Dutch pattern: the verb is *opstaan* (to get up), but *op* is thrown to the **end of the sentence**. Think of English "I get *up*" — except in Dutch the *up* travels all the way to the end. Writing *ik opsta* is wrong.
**Ik kleed me aan** — two things at once: the verb is separable (*aankleden*) **and** reflexive (*me*). The order: verb, reflexive word, the rest, then the separated part at the end.

**Ik ontbijt** — the verb *ontbijten* (to have breakfast) doesn't split, even though it starts with *ont-*. Prefixes that never split: *be-*, *ge-*, *ver-*, *ont-*, *her-*, *er-*. All other prefixes split.
**Ik pak de trein** — in Dutch you "grab" the train, much like English *take the train*. The alternative is *met de trein gaan*.
**Ik sta pas om acht uur op** — *pas* means "not until / only" in a time sense: *pas om acht uur* = not until eight. Don't confuse it with *net* (just): *hij is net weg*.
**Om de hoek** = around the corner, i.e. very close — the same image as in English.
**Daarom ben ik altijd moe** — the sentence opens with *daarom* (that's why), so the verb jumps in front of the subject. Once again the Unit 10 rule, which is starting to show up everywhere.

grammars.title: Separable verbs
body: A large group of Dutch verbs consists of a verb + a prefix that can stand on its own (*op*, *aan*, *mee*, *uit*, *af*, *terug*) — like English phrasal verbs (*get up*, *call back*). In a simple sentence that prefix **always moves to the end**.

head: Dictionary form
Meaning
In a sentence
rows: De trein komt om acht uur **aan**.

after: When there's a helper verb, the separable verb **joins back together** at the end: *Ik moet om zeven uur **opstaan**.* This rule becomes very useful from Unit 13 on.
The stress falls on the prefix: **OP**staan, **AAN**komen. That's the quickest way to tell whether a verb is separable — compare ver**TEL**len, stressed further back, which never splits.
⚠️ The meanings can be far apart: *opnemen* (to pick up the phone) versus *nemen* (to take), *uitgaan* (to go out) versus *gaan* (to go). Treat each separable verb as a new word, not a variation.

grammars.title: Reflexive verbs
body: Some actions that stand alone in English ("to wash", "to get dressed", "to feel") need a reflexive word in Dutch — the doer acts on themselves, as in English "to enjoy yourself".
after: The most common ones: *zich wassen* (to wash), *zich aankleden* (to get dressed), *zich voelen* (to feel), *zich haasten* (to hurry), *zich vergissen* (to be mistaken), *zich vervelen* (to be bored).
*Ik voel me niet lekker* = "I don't feel well" — a sentence that will save you at the pharmacy and at the office.
⚠️ Don't add a reflexive word to verbs that don't need one. *Ik douche* is already correct; *ik douche me* sounds odd.

blocks.title: Linking your story
items: *eerst … dan … en daarna …* is enough to tell a whole day.
⚠️ All these linking words stand **at the start of the sentence**, and as soon as one is in front, the verb jumps to second place: *Daarna **pak** ik de trein.*
*Meestal*, *altijd*, *soms*, *nooit* say how often: *Ik kook meestal zelf.*

head: Nederlands
When
What
rows: a hot meal, the only one of the day

blocks.text: Two things surprise newcomers. **First**, lunch in the Netherlands is almost always cold: two slices of bread with cheese, brought from home in a box (*een broodtrommel*). **Second**, dinner starts at half past five — an hour that in many countries still feels like the afternoon.

*Hagelslag* — chocolate sprinkles on buttered bread — is eaten by adults without the slightest guilt, and the Dutch eat more of it than any other country. If there's one Dutch eating habit worth trying, this is it.
Sentences you'll often hear at the table: *Smakelijk eten!* (enjoy your meal), *Wil je nog wat?* (would you like some more?), *Ik zit vol* (I'm full), *Het was heerlijk* (that was delicious).

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentences with the separable verb in the right places.
Fill in the right reflexive word (me, je, zich, ons).

items: I take the train to work.
I go to bed around midnight.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
items: op / zes / sta / uur / ik / om
bed / ga / ik / naar / twaalf / om

answers: sta … op — komt … aan — gaan … uit — belt … op — bel … terug
Ik sta om zeven uur op. — Daarna ontbijt ik. — Ik ga met de trein naar mijn werk. — 's Avonds kook ik. — Ik ga rond middernacht naar bed. — Ik voel me niet lekker.
Ik sta om zes uur op. — Daarna pak ik de trein. — Ik kleed me aan. — Ik ga om twaalf naar bed. — Ik ben altijd moe.
